official_metadata.title: Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report
official_metadata.abstract: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.

source_quote.text: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments.

source_body_quotes.quote: To develop the agentic capabilities required for scientific work, we build a large collection of verifiable environments. The tasks range from general-purpose tool use, search, and coding to workflows involving machine learning experiments and interaction with scientific software. Task-specific checks assess outcomes using evidence such as execution results, changes in environment state, and submitted artifacts. We use XTuner [ 20 ] as our post-training framework.

We treat the scientific interface as a trainable component of the model’s reasoning policy. Following supervised initialization, we refine modality-specific projectors through reinforcement learning, using verifiable scientific outcomes as rewards. The scientific encoders and language backbone remain frozen, so task feedback shapes how evidence is presented to the backbone and used to answer scientific questions.

Sage S2.1 Flash brings native scientific inputs and interactive agent capabilities into a general-purpose model. Scientific modality adaptation trains the projectors to present scientific evidence to the shared backbone, while training in verifiable environments gives the model feedback on whether its actions achieve the task objective.

official_metadata.title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models
official_metadata.abstract: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/

official_metadata.title: AllocFlow: End-to-End Portfolio Trading Action Generation from Raw Market Data
official_metadata.abstract: Real-world portfolio management requires converting noisy market observations into coordinated, simultaneous allocations across multiple assets under shared capital constraints. Advances in forecasting models and alpha discovery help identify opportunities. However, traditional pipelines often decouple signal forecasting from portfolio construction, potentially misaligning learning with allocation and execution objectives. We present AllocFlow, an end-to-end flow-matching framework that directly generates joint portfolio allocations from raw multi-asset market histories. To capture dependencies among portfolio positions, AllocFlow employs a cross-asset flow Transformer conditioned on temporal market representations to generate continuous, signed position weights across all instruments jointly. To address the sample inefficiency and instability of learning continuous allocation policies from scratch, we establish a two-stage training scheme: strategy-supervised imitation shapes a structured distribution of candidate portfolios, followed by group-relative reinforcement learning (RL) that refines joint decisions using portfolio-level financial rewards and a frozen policy reference. On hourly cryptocurrency perpetual futures, RL refinement raises the annualized net return of the imitation policy from $27.79\%$ to $51.38\%$ and its Calmar ratio from $0.955$ to $4.043$, surpassing the teacher strategy on every metric, and AllocFlow reaches a Calmar ratio of $4.90$ on six further months of unseen 2026 data without retraining.

official_metadata.title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
official_metadata.abstract: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

official_metadata.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
official_metadata.abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .005. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

source_body_quotes.quote: We build I I from the tools’ declared types, never from text. Tool and argument roles come from one fixed lexicon per benchmark: verb prefixes mark read-only, writing, destructive, and granting tools, argument names mark targets and principals, and a short list names the tools that write only to the user’s own calendar or drive. The executor captures the return of each read-only tool as the typed object the tool produced, before it is serialized for the model, and indexes a value only when its declared field type is an identity format (email, URI, UUID, hostname, IP) or its field has a routing role (recipient, sender, participant, channel).

The closest sibling is ROPE ( Ma et al., 2026b ) , whose deterministic origin check guards an audited set of sensitive parameters after a router reads each request. SPILLWAY takes a lighter point: a flat typed-identity floor fixed by the tool schemas and a role lexicon, with no per-task router and lighter than the per-step dependency state of APPA ( Kravchenko et al., 2026 ) or AgentArmor ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and the per-argument provenance of PACT ( Fan et al., 2026 ) , and a judge bounded by ingress evidence. CommandSans ( Das et al., 2025 ) learns a token-level sanitizer for tool outputs. Tool-input and tool-output firewalls ( Bhagwatkar et al., 2025 ) run an LLM on every tool input and output and filter content, with no check on where an effect goes. They report zero on the standard attack, but their own adaptive cascade raises their sanitizer’s attack success to 30 % 30\% (Slack). Agent data injection ( Choi et al., 2026 ) spoofs trusted metadata inside untrusted text, such as a forged author field in a comment body, and succeeds against most defenses it tests except CaMeL’s strict policy. A spoofed value in a typed field is the case of Sec. 7 . SPILLWAY’s floor and sanitizer use no model, and its only model call is a bounded judge, under one call per benign episode on qwen3:8b (Figure 3 ). With its deterministic floor, SPILLWAY holds in-scope attack success at .000 .000 under a forged chat template and at .005 .005 on average under a frontier reinforcement-learning attacker (PISmith), where content filtering alone does not (Tables 4 , 7 ).

official_metadata.title: SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations
official_metadata.abstract: A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. Requirement-level trajectory analysis reveals failures throughout the delivery process: Claude-Opus-5.5 directs a mean of 93% of first questions about queried cards to their accountable owners across runs but obtains only 64% of colleague-held requirements. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.

official_metadata.title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters
official_metadata.abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.

official_metadata.title: PaperCritic: Training AI Reviewers to Assess the Soundness of Papers
official_metadata.abstract: As AI conference submissions grow rapidly, AI reviewers are being considered as an alternative. However, simply imitating human reviewing is problematic because reviewing serves multiple purposes, including evaluating papers' soundness, interestingness, and clarity, the last two of which are subjective. In this work, we focus solely on evaluating soundness, the most important and objective criterion, and define the learning objective as jointly maximizing (1) precision, based on the soundness and substantiveness of review points, and (2) recall, the coverage of high-quality reference review points. Under this problem formulation, we construct a quality-labeled review point dataset, PaperSound-23K, using 1K ICLR submissions and 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points. Using this dataset, we train an AI reviewer model, PaperCritic, through reinforcement learning with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward. Our experiments show that PaperCritic outperforms frontier models and models trained with other AI reviewer training methods on an in-domain test set. Surprisingly, learning to review ICLR submissions also transfers to reviewing Nature-family papers and even to out-of-domain reviewing tasks (e.g., code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing).

official_metadata.title: VoxMel TTS Technical Report
official_metadata.abstract: Continuous autoregressive TTS relies on an acoustic target that enables stable next-latent modeling while preserving fine-grained acoustic details. While existing approaches employ learned compressed representations (e.g., continuous VAE latents) to render prediction tractable, they rely on complex neural encoders that often cap generation fidelity. Conversely, training-free targets like mel-spectrograms eliminate encoder overhead, yet their potential for autoregressive generation remains largely underexplored. In this work, we propose VoxMel, a tokenizer-free framework for autoregressive TTS that makes stable mel modeling tractable through a fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar transform. The transform first decomposes each mel spectrogram along frequency into local averages and a frequency residual, then splits the averaged component along time into Coarse-Mel and a temporal residual. A language-model backbone with a flow-matching head autoregressively generates Coarse-Mel. Non-autoregressive residual tiers then predict the temporal residual from Coarse-Mel, followed by the frequency residual conditioned on the reconstructed Frequency-Averaged Mel. Neither residual is fed back into the autoregressive history. Trained on 100K hours of Emilia, the supervised 0.6B model obtains 1.51\% WER and 0.738 speaker similarity (SIM) on test-en, and 1.29\% CER and 0.755 SIM on test-zh. GRPO improves these results to 1.15\% WER / 0.753 SIM and 1.17\% CER / 0.776 SIM, respectively. We also distill the guided flow head into two- and four-step students, requiring 2 or 4 head evaluations per coarse frame. The four-step student retains competitive SIM and nearly matches the supervised model in WER/CER.

official_metadata.title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization
official_metadata.abstract: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

source_body_quotes.quote: 2.1 Task Definition and Optimization Scope Unlike benchmarks built around isolated historical commits or patches ( Shetty et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ) , we define each task by a complete application workload and its required outputs. Each task fixes the target computation and leaves agents to decide where and how to optimize. We evaluate performance across the full workflow, so local improvements count only if they reduce total runtime. Figure 2: Score@1 by application area. Benchmark v1.1, first run of the 16 agents in Table 1 ; top six agents per area, increasing clockwise. Labels give the top three scores (%); each sector is scaled to its own maximum (dashed arc). Claude Opus 5.5’s three runs stopped by the provider’s safety system, on two Transport tasks and one Numerics task, count as zero (Table 1 ). Each task provides a working baseline implementation, build and execution scripts, task instructions, and a public testing interface in a container with fixed CPU core and memory limits (Appendix D ). Agents may modify application source code, compiler options, and dependencies within the permitted directory, while preserving the required computations and outputs. Application-level optimization means reducing the end-to-end runtime of this prescribed workflow under these resource limits. Figure 1 illustrates this workflow with \tasknamebox Ag SU2: agents optimize an airfoil flow simulation by editing solver routines, common libraries, and compilation flags. To pass, each run must complete all 250 iterations on the supplied 10,216-element mesh and produce five complete flow-field snapshots. The public test rebuilds the candidate, runs the simulation, and checks field residuals and run-to-run consistency against reference solutions. The verifier alone controls the validation meshes, physical configurations, and the checking code used to score submissions. Timing boundaries follow each task’s computational workflow, excluding one-time setup and build steps; end-to-end runtime in this paper means this timed workflow, and build time is reported separately. For example, \tasknamebox Ag GROMACS times the mdrun simulation, excluding build time and topology preparation; the \tasknamebox Ag HPCG-derived task times sparse matrix assembly, initialization, multigrid solves, and output; and \tasknamebox Ag paged generation times model loading, autoregressive decoding, checkpoint saving, and recovery in a new process. Because these stages are timed and checked together, a faster kernel counts only in proportion to its share of the workflow, and a shortcut that skips a required output or recovery step fails correctness rather than earning a speedup. Appendix Table 12 gives representative contracts, and Table 10 lists each task’s CPU cores, memory, and time limits; every task package specifies its own outputs and checks.

7 Limitations Task coverage and baselines. The evaluation covers CPU workflows at the specified scales and resource budgets. Speedups are relative to task-provided baselines with varying degrees of tuning; they measure improvement from those starting points. Some speedups exploit structure in the specified workload, such as the \tasknamebox Ag HPCG-derived operator, which admits a direct solver; the tasks measure whether agents find and realize such opportunities, and results at other scales, on other hardware, and in production environments require separate evaluation. Agent and execution settings. As in other agent benchmarks, each result reflects a model running in its harness, so score differences combine model capability with harness behavior, inference compute, and execution conditions. Every agent receives the same task container, resource and time limits, and timing and correctness rules, and scores are runtime ratios to the task baseline. Table 1 reports one run per agent, and repeated runs cover two agents (Appendix A.3 ). Separating models from harnesses and measuring sensitivity to hardware placement are natural extensions that the retained programs and containers support. Benchmark versions. Results of v1.0 and v1.1 are reported separately and never combined; v1.1 revised the task statements and fixed several verifier, timing and environment problems (Appendix A ). The trajectory analyses use v1.0 runs. Trajectory samples. The trajectory analyses cover five agents. Source labels combine model-assisted annotation with targeted source checks, and prevalence estimates rest on reviewed samples. Version histories cover 31 runs in seven applications, most candidates have one timing observation, and controlled experiments establish effects for the tested artifacts, workloads, and settings.

official_metadata.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
official_metadata.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

official_metadata.title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
official_metadata.abstract: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

official_metadata.title: MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos
official_metadata.abstract: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.

official_metadata.title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
official_metadata.abstract: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.

official_metadata.title: Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model
official_metadata.abstract: Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345$\times$ less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

official_metadata.title: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late
official_metadata.abstract: Coding agents can solve a task well before they stop working on it. We characterize \emph{termination lag}--the number of steps between an agent's first correct patch and the end of its run--across five models, two agent frameworks, and three SWE-bench datasets by recording and testing every distinct repository patch generated during execution. Our analysis reveals that 38--82% of successful runs achieve a correct solution on their initial source-code edit. However, agents continue to expend substantial effort after correct patches, with post-solution steps accounting for a median of 35--37% for Qwen3-Coder and 54--60% for Laguna-XS.2 in successful runs on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Agents spend most of these additional steps verifying their work and exploring the repository. In a small fraction of cases (1--8%), this continued activity leads agents to undo their earlier correct patch, leaving the final solution incorrect.

official_metadata.title: Correcting Persistent Failures in Point-Cloud Grasping Policies using Human Demonstrations in Virtual Reality
official_metadata.abstract: Robots in homes, warehouses and farms must pick up objects they have never seen, usually without a 3D model or a category label. A grasping policy that works directly on the point cloud from a depth sensor needs only the geometry the robot observes, so it applies to any new object. Offline grasp generators such as Contact-GraspNet work this way, but they rank grasps by learned plausibility rather than by whether the grasp actually lifts the object. Reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize for that directly and make a point-cloud grasping policy much better on average, yet it leaves specific grasps persistently unsolved. We present a human-in-the-loop failure loop that targets those grasps: situations an RL policy keeps failing are mined automatically, sent to a virtual-reality application where a person picks the object up with their own hands, and returned to training as two grasp points. The person contributes only where to grasp; the robot chooses its own approach. In simulation, RL raises success on unseen objects from 55% with Contact-GraspNet to 83%. Adding 58 human demonstrations nearly doubles success on the hard cases RL kept failing, from 24% to 45%, and recovers performance that RL alone loses on similar cases that were never demonstrated, without reducing success on unseen objects.

official_metadata.title: Continuation-Guided LLM Evolution of Program Policies and Goal Compilers in Craftax
official_metadata.abstract: Coding agents can synthesize and optimize code-based policies from simulator feedback, allowing the resulting program to act with zero inference model calls. But for long horizon tasks, two challenges arise: local improvements can hurt final success and switching to a new objective requires another expensive synthesis run. We propose a framework that first develops competence by refining the policy through a feedback cascade, moving from episode returns to hierarchical goals and belief updates which can be scored densely from simulator. In the Craftax game, a partially observed and procedurally generated environment, refinements via episode level feedback stall at <1% final-level arrival, whereas with the feedback cascade the optimized policy reaches the final stage 50% of time (28% final boss defeats). Furthermore, to make this competence reusable towards new goals, we factor the previous controller into an environment interpreter $I$ (models, memory, skills) and a rule program $p_0$, and we show that coding agents can optimize a reusable goal compiler $C_θ$ that maps structured tasks $g$ into new rule programs $p_g$. Across five independent compiler searches trained only on short tasks, the resulting compilers successfully transfer zero-shot to longer tasks without any task-specific tuning nor inference-time LLM calls: continuation-scored feedback and a fixed machine with an editable program together turn a single-task competent policy into a reusable one. As an example, take a held-out task g g with four stages: reach floor 1, return to the surface (floor 0), acquire six coal while maintaining at least two coal, and then reach floor 2 (Figure 1 , bottom; full source in Appendix C.1 ). Limitations. First, the lineage is a single adaptive development history. The authors introduced each regime when the diagnosis suggested it, so the feedback is confounded with ancestry, though several controls experiments were performed. Second, the synthesized interpreter is a Craftax-specific implementation with a lot of inherited knowledge, and parity is an empirical check on held-out worlds. Third, goal generalization is restricted to a supplied language and one game engine. The composition and progress semantics come from the infrastructure and each per-task baseline is a single search.

4 Related Work Programmatic reinforcement learning searches over structured policy spaces ( Verma et al. 2018 ; Trivedi et al. 2021 ; Liu et al. 2023 ) , and language-model-guided search adds code proposals made by a language model ( Liu et al. 2025 ) . Code as Policies generates executable control from instructions, Voyager develops reusable skills, and WorldCoder writes executable world models ( Liang et al. 2023 ; Wang et al. 2023 ; Tang et al. 2024 ) . In our case, the object that is deployed is a frozen program-to-program map over a supplied goal language, and the language model only takes part in development. FunSearch and AlphaEvolve combine edits written by a model with automated evaluation ( Romera-Paredes et al. 2024 ; Novikov et al. 2025 ) . Dense feedback can expose failures that look the same under a scalar score ( Gallego 2026 ) . Our feedback cascade also changes the starting state of the comparison, the scope of the code and the continuation. Saved-state branching is related to restoring states for exploration ( Ecoffet et al. 2021 ) , although here the paired continuations are used to evaluate local program edits against the chosen endpoint. Options and hierarchies of machines formalize temporally extended behavior and partial control programs ( Sutton et al. 1999 ; Parr and Russell 1998 ) . MAXQ distinguishes the recursive optimality of a subtask from the performance of the whole hierarchy, and ALisp takes into account what follows a subroutine through its exit value ( Dietterich 2000 ; Andre and Russell 2002 ) . Our continuation formulation applies the same distinction to the edits of coding agents and to handoffs between programs. Policy sketches and reward machines also expose task structure for composition ( Andreas et al. 2017 ; Toro Icarte et al. 2022 ) . In our case the task semantics and the monitor are given, and the code search adapts how the controller uses the skills it already has. The resource guards are similar to runtime shields ( Alshiekh et al. 2018 ) , but without a synthesized guarantee on the winning region. Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains a single network over a goal space, and the generalization comes from universal value function approximators and hindsight relabeling ( Schaul et al. 2015 ; Andrychowicz et al. 2017 ; Liu et al. 2022 ) . In Craftax, Matthews et al. (2026) train neural policies over a discrete set of semantic goals by outputting values for all goals at once (LEO). Our goal compiler can be seen as a programmatic family of goal-conditioned policies: the goal enters through code generation over a fixed machine instead of as a network input or output head, the generated program can be inspected and runs without a model, and generalization is tested on multi-stage compositions with constraints that are longer than any seen in training.

official_metadata.title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
official_metadata.abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

official_metadata.title: Ego Guidance: Enhancing Robot Policy Learning with Action-Free Human Egocentric Videos
official_metadata.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision. Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction. We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales. We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.

official_metadata.title: Marimba: A System One Model for Speech
official_metadata.abstract: Speech applications require decisions about term presence, turn completion, and language within an audio window. We present Marimba, an interface for typed speech decisions built on frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B features. Lexical questions use zero-shot scoring of ASR transcripts; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head and a separate layer-18 turn-end readout. Language identification uses the ASR model's own language scores. On private conversational test sets, decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92; on public read speech it is 0.92-0.97. Speech Commands four-way accuracy is 0.93; binary lexical ECE is at most 0.08. Personal-information detection, which passes the greedy transcript to a private, curated PII pipeline, reaches item-level F1 0.904 on synthetic Brazilian Portuguese speech (1.000 on reference transcripts). Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on AMI and VoxConverse, above an ECAPA baseline, and count speakers (0, 1, 2, or 3+) more accurately than pyannote 3.1. The turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set. On a subset of ICSI meetings labeled by next speaker, AUROC is 0.716 versus 0.712; the paired confidence interval includes zero.

official_metadata.title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination
official_metadata.abstract: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.

official_metadata.title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
official_metadata.abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.

official_metadata.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
official_metadata.abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

Category A (Greedy Single-Pass Baselines): Multi-agent architectures are compared against a single forward pass ( N = 1 , T = 1 N=1,T=1 ). This comparison provides baseline performance but confounds coordination with sample count and test-time token expenditure. 2. Category B (Sample-Matched Baselines): The number of generation trajectories is matched ( k = N k=N ), such as in k k -sample self-consistency with majority voting. Total tokens, latency, and monetary costs remain unconstrained. This category evaluates whether communication provides advantages beyond independent sample multiplicity. 3. Category C (Resource-Matched Baselines): A declared resource constraint is held equal between conditions, such as matched thinking tokens ( R reason MAS = R reason SAS R_{\text{reason}}^{\text{MAS}}=R_{\text{reason}}^{\text{SAS}} ), matched sample or iteration ceilings ( R sample MAS = R sample SAS R_{\text{sample}}^{\text{MAS}}=R_{\text{sample}}^{\text{SAS}} ), or matched monetary budgets ( R cost MAS = R cost SAS R_{\text{cost}}^{\text{MAS}}=R_{\text{cost}}^{\text{SAS}} ). 4. Category D (Pareto Frontier Sweeps): Accuracy is evaluated against inference expenditure across a parametric sweep of configurations, tracing empirical accuracy–cost or accuracy–latency frontiers (e.g., Wunderlich et al. [12] ). Comparing multi-agent teams against greedy single-agent baselines mixes two phenomena: variance reduction from drawing multiple stochastic trajectories, and coordination through communication. Under token matching or iteration controls (Category C), the comparison holds compute constant, isolating coordination efficiency. Under matching on agent count (Category B), the comparison reflects unconstrained sample multiplicity, where majority voting over independent samples matches or exceeds debate without communication overhead [ 13 , 15 ] .

7 Conclusion Across 9 studies comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations, multi-agent systems show no consistent advantage once single-agent baselines receive repeated samples or matched compute budgets. Against baselines matched on sample count or budget the mean difference is − 0.042 -0.042 (REML β ^ = − 0.195 \hat{\beta}=-0.195 , CR2 95% CI [ − 0.320 -0.320 , − 0.070 -0.070 ]), and the multi-agent system’s accuracy equals or falls below its baseline’s in 74% of the 474 contrasts ( Table 2 ). The one positive exception among extracted studies is Wunderlich et al. [12] , at comparable compute read off Pareto fronts, not an exact budget match. The sampling gap is below zero in all 5 studies that report both baselines ( Section 5.3 ). Architectural coordination cannot be demonstrated without holding test-time compute constant. Practitioners should allocate single agents equal inference budgets before deploying multi-agent pipelines, and reserve multi-agent topologies for tasks in which communication can add something. official_metadata.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
official_metadata.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.

official_metadata.title: JEPA4R: Embodied JEPA World Models with 4D Point Planning
official_metadata.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space. Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning. We present JEPA4R, a JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through a policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning. A decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps. Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Trained only in a digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand.

official_metadata.title: Dataset Distillation via Drifting
official_metadata.abstract: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set of samples such that they directly approximate the per-class data distribution. Specifically, we "drift" our distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor such that they move both toward the real data and away from each other without using a classification objective. We find that our drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods while still serving as powerful training samples for classification. Furthermore, we showcase our method's use as a visualization tool for better interpreting models and extend it beyond images to other modalities. Our work advances the frontier of dataset distillation, offering a novel synthesis method and proposing distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation. More broadly, our findings help address the growing need to understand both data and models by uncovering more about how they interact.

official_metadata.title: Correct Labels Are Not Enough: Reliable Metadata Can Silently Control Model Behavior
official_metadata.abstract: Fine-tuning data can include metadata that predicts the correct answer, such as a reward-model score or a quality label. We ask whether a model learns to rely on this metadata even when every training label is correct. We fine-tune 7-9B open-weight models from three families on multiple-choice questions in which (Reward: 5) always marks the correct option; when this annotation is moved to a wrong option at test time, models select that option on 97-100% of CommonsenseQA items. Removing it leaves most answers correct, so evaluation without it misses the dependence. Cue-following rises sharply with training-time reliability and develops even with neutral or nonsense annotation words, although test-time wording affects its strength. A Qwen3 experiment also finds cue dependence in option-letter scores after direct preference optimization. Audits can test for this dependence by moving or removing visible annotations while holding the task and correct answer fixed.

official_metadata.title: Invariant-Aware Harness Enforcement to Protect LLM Agents from Silent API Failures
official_metadata.abstract: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. It ignores part of a request, such as a misnamed filter, yet returns HTTP 200 and a plausible but wrong result. Current fixes, such as checklists, reviewer models and LLM judges, ask the model to catch it. But models often see the problem and answer anyway. We present SilentGuard, which moves the decision from the model to the harness running tool calls. It tests each result against invariants that any correct API must satisfy and withholds values that break one. We find silent failures in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691 times. Current fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, and agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. Across 7 open models, SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on its target faults from 74.0% to 1.7%, with no loss on fault-free tasks. On three frontier models they fall from 70.2% to 0.5%. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

official_metadata.title: When Expert Disagreement Hurts: Prestige and Selectivity in LLM Decision Revision
official_metadata.abstract: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers. We introduce a controlled two-pass audit that holds the question, the evidence, and the model's initial answer fixed and varies only the revision context: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a domain expert. For binary decisions the accounting is exact: revision raises accuracy only if it is selective enough, reversing wrong answers more than $a/(1-a)$ times as often as correct ones, where $a$ is initial accuracy (nine times at 90%). Across five models and 1,989 evidence-grounded decisions in medicine, science, and law, no model clears this bar under expert disagreement, and accuracy falls by up to 16.1 points. The expert label, a prestige cue, adds reversals for four of the five models, yet its effect on accuracy ranges from a 5.2-point loss to a 2.4-point gain, so reversal counts are a poor proxy for harm. With identical arguments from both sources, the label still raises reversal for three proprietary models and in a pooled analysis of four newer models. Models also respond to stated source reliability. Revision pipelines should therefore be evaluated with paired, conditional metrics, per model and protocol.

official_metadata.title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control
official_metadata.abstract: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

official_metadata.title: Centered Ablation: Why Last-Layer Directional Ablation Under-Fires or Collapses, and a Closed-Form Fix
official_metadata.abstract: Directional ablation removes a hidden state's component along a "behaviour direction" while a language model runs. It is the standard way to switch a behaviour such as refusal off, but it is erratic: on some models it barely fires, on others the text collapses into repetition. We show why, and fix it. At the last residual stream, ablation is exactly a logit bias: a fixed vocabulary footprint scaled by a gate, the cosine between the hidden state and the direction. The gate is measured from the origin, but last-layer states share a large common mode far from it, so a direction that overlaps the common mode fires on benign text and under-fires on its targets. Centered Ablation (CA) projects the common mode out of the direction, in closed form. Across 8 models, CA raises attack success by 29 and 46 points where the standard recipe under-fires, cuts collapse on Gemma-2-9B from 50\% to 1\%, and preserves 12 to 40 points more benign answers on high-overlap models, 39 to 46 more than the affine offset of prior work. Two numbers computed before generation predict, on models the analysis had not seen, which gain faithfulness and which gain attack success, and a collapse index marks when text degenerates. We also show that two standard safety judges score collapsed text in opposite directions, which can fabricate a 46-point effect.

official_metadata.title: UMM-JEPA: Generative Pretraining via Masked Next-Scale Representation Prediction for Unified Multimodal Models
official_metadata.abstract: Unified multimodal models can support both visual understanding and generation, yet generative training does not necessarily improve understanding. We argue that this limitation may arise from a mismatch between the representation targeted by generation and the perceptual representation used for understanding. Conventional generation objectives primarily optimize synthesis-oriented spaces such as discrete visual codes or generative latents. We therefore introduce UMM-JEPA, which reformulates generation as progressive prediction of continuous visual-understanding representations. The model constructs a multi-scale representation hierarchy from coarse to fine, while pixel rendering is decoupled from representation pretraining and attached only afterward. Controlled comparisons show that the representation-prediction objective accounts for most of the understanding improvement, while a data-matched control leaves the group means nearly unchanged. UMM-JEPA reaches a 16-benchmark visual mean of 51.71, against 46.36 for the understanding-only Qwen-VL baseline, and the text mean also rises. Compared with discrete-code and latent-flow generation objectives, perceptual representation prediction yields stronger and more consistent transfer to understanding. Linear probes and visual-evidence interventions further reveal richer object and spatial structure and stronger use of image-specific information. These results suggest that generation can benefit understanding when it directly supervises the perceptual representations that understanding consumes.

official_metadata.title: GlyphAtlas: Disentangling Stroke Detail from Layout for Scene Text Synthesis
official_metadata.abstract: Scene text synthesis requires stroke-accurate characters rendered in a specified layout, as well as visual coherence with the surrounding scene. To achieve this, existing methods commonly pre-render the target text at its intended locations to form a glyph image that jointly specifies layout and glyph structure. However, this representation ties the resolution of each glyph to its target region, limiting fine-grained stroke guidance for small, densely packed, or structurally complex text. To tackle this, we propose GlyphAtlas, a scene text synthesis framework that retains the glyph image as a spatial anchor and supplies fine-grained stroke references through a dedicated glyph atlas. The atlas renders and encodes each character or word in a separate cell, decoupling reference resolution from target-region size. We further introduce atlas-anchored attention, which lets each text region retrieve stroke detail only from its corresponding atlas cells to refine the coarse glyph structure provided by the glyph image. This coarse-to-fine conditioning simplifies stroke rendering while preserving explicit layout correspondence. We optimize GlyphAtlas with a mask-weighted flow matching objective and a timestep-weighted text perceptual loss for writing accuracy and background consistency. Random resolution augmentation of atlas cells supports adjustable atlas budgets at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GlyphAtlas achieves stroke-accurate synthesis of small, dense, and structurally complex text, zero-shot transfer to languages unseen during task-specific training, and leading performance in scenes with many text regions. project page: https://fr0zencrane.github.io/project-glyphatlas/

official_metadata.title: ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization
official_metadata.abstract: Visual agents answer questions about ultra-high-resolution photos by zooming into the relevant regions. However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. We propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO), which trains agents on contrast sets. A contrast set asks one question about several versions of an image that differ only in a small region with the evidence and have different answers, so only reading the evidence solves the whole set. CrossRPO rewards solving the whole set, and we prove that it does not reinforce a set answered from common sense. We build contrast sets for training (ViRA-Train) and evaluation (ViRA-Bench) by editing one small object in images of 21 to 120 megapixels, and we photograph further sets with real changes (ViRA-Bench-Real) to exclude editing traces. We train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, with CrossRPO on only about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. ViRA-9B is the most accurate open model of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, both at their highest thinking level, on most benchmarks.

official_metadata.title: Reflection Anchors for Propagation-Aware Visual Retention in Long-Chain Multimodal Reasoning
official_metadata.abstract: Long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improves large vision--language models, but visual information often fades during generation, limiting long-horizon multimodal reasoning. Existing methods either re-inject vision at inference or train policies for stronger grounding, but where to intervene relies on perception heuristics rather than principled gain analysis, and how local visual influence propagates remains implicit. We study this problem from an information-theoretic standpoint and derive a lower bound on the downstream visual gain of a one-step intervention, which suggests two factors: local branching room (token entropy) and downstream visual propagation potential (suffix divergence from a vision-marginalized reference). Guided by this analysis, we propose reflection-anchor policy optimization (RAPO), a GRPO-based policy optimization method that selects high-entropy reflection anchors and optimizes a chain-masked finite-window KL surrogate for downstream visual dependence. Experiments on reasoning-intensive and general-domain benchmarks show that RAPO delivers substantial gains over strong baselines across multiple LVLM backbones. Mechanism analyses further indicate that reflection anchors are enriched for visually sensitive decision points and that RAPO increases contrastive visual-dependence signals along generated trajectories.

official_metadata.title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents
official_metadata.abstract: We built a hybrid multi-agent trading system that combines large language model (LLM) analysts with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. Company-news and macroeconomic agents return structured reports to a coordinator that sets stock weights and cash reserves. We evaluate the portfolio engine using its broker-recorded paper account, which operated with deterministic fallbacks, and compare LLM-enabled configurations through retrospective replays. From March 11 to August 28, 2026, the account returned 34.5%, compared with 14.4% for the S&P 500 fund SPY over the same dates. This raw return advantage came with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies also finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred to the next. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation, and response contracts. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.

source_body_quotes.quote: 3.2 Specialist Reports and Explicit Allocation Authority We implemented the two analyst roles using Claude Haiku 4.5, with separate task contexts, response fields, and deterministic fallbacks. The company sentiment agent reads headlines with price and sector context, returning a score and confidence. The macro agent reads cross-market indicators and market news, returning a score and an action label, or stance . Using one base model keeps the service choice fixed; the task and context distinguish the roles. We assign each report a defined role in the coordinator. In the advisory configuration, we use sentiment in the composite for stock weights. Its nominal coefficient within that composite is 0.15. The macro score is blended equally with a numerical macro score and also enters the trend analyzer. The blended score affects both weights and cash. The stance remains a reported recommendation. This arrangement gives the agents defined input channels while preserving a common selection and allocation procedure. We implemented three allocator configurations to vary analyst authority (Figure 3 ). The deterministic baseline, L0, uses fallbacks for both roles. The advisory arm, L1, enables analyst scores at the interfaces just described. The sizing arm, L2, retains the advisory stock inputs but replaces score-based cash with a fixed stance-to-cash mapping. This last change delegates an exposure decision, so it creates a different portfolio policy even when the reports themselves are unchanged. Figure 3: Report handling and allocation authority. Usable model fields or deterministic fallbacks reach a specified portfolio policy. L0 bypasses model calls. L1 uses analyst scores, while L2 additionally maps the macro stance to cash. Parsing and numeric handling are component-specific (Appendix C ). Fallback preserves an allocation path; it does not establish equivalent information quality. We keep coordination in software to make the allocation policy inspectable and to control how analyst reports affect capital. The cost is that information outside the accepted fields cannot alter the portfolio. An explanation cannot override the selector, and a stance affects cash only in the sizing configuration. The implemented system has neither peer dialogue nor a learned coordinator.

3.3 Cash Reserves and Stateful Execution We use a discrete reserve policy to connect the macro assessment to market exposure. The advisory allocator rounds the blended score to one decimal and maps it to four cash levels, with a maximum reserve of 20%. The target therefore remains mostly invested. Discrete levels make the policy explicit but concentrate its sensitivity near boundaries. For the sizing configuration, we replace this score rule with a stance-to-cash map that permits a wider action set. We implemented execution as a state-dependent transition from current holdings to the target. The executor blends that adjustment, applies minimum-trade conditions, and processes sells before buys. Small changes can remain untraded, while partial exits can leave residual holdings. The resulting book can therefore contain more names than the ten-stock target. This distinction is important when interpreting concentration, turnover, and the feedback into future selection. Execution also changed during the historical window. Earlier versions used partial exits and permitted margin. A later version combined the rank buffer with full exits and a larger minimum-trade condition; the final version added a cash-budget guard. Faster adjustment would track the target more closely but could increase trading burden. The observed version sequence is reconstructed rather than treated as one uniform execution policy. Appendix H reports the resulting differences between the account and the replay.

3.4 Response Contracts and Selective Calls We require machine-readable fields at the analyst interface and implement a deterministic fallback for unusable replies. The parsers handle scores and confidence according to component-specific numeric rules; they do not execute free-text sizing guidance. Explanatory fields make reports easier to inspect, but compete for the response budget needed by the allocation fields. We test shorter contracts for both parsing reliability and changes in recommendations. We also evaluate an optional call gate using information available before a macro request. Distance from the numerical macro score to a cash threshold indicates when a model-induced shift could change the reserve. We compare this rule with input-based date selection. The direct readout is the share of the full advisory arm’s allocation distance occurring on selected dates. Separate replays gate both roles or macro alone. These are offline comparisons; their trading consequences have not been measured prospectively.

4.3 Design Comparisons Cash-policy controls, including every tested constant reserve, examine how much of a sizing result can be explained by exposure. The 5% control is chosen from the model’s modal action rather than optimized for return. It uses baseline stock scores, so it approximately matches exposure without matching the full policy. Full-window paired return comparisons resample 119 return intervals, including the initial day, with a circular five-date block check. Intervals describe within-window uncertainty. Further comparisons replace an analyst with its fallback, vary allocation coefficients and cash boundaries, or change the requested response fields. These are component and rule ablations ( Meyes et al., 2019 ) . Portfolio-distance definitions, same-state comparisons, and exact configurations are in Appendix I . Two responses were collected per historical prompt; primary replays use the first. Attempt-level and final-task failures have separate denominators because historical collection allows retries, while production can fall back after a failure.

6.2 Scope and Next Evaluation Our evaluation covers one paper portfolio, one historical window, and one primary LLM provider. The protocol details the reconstruction and model-knowledge limits. The next-session test addresses a specific timing inconsistency by changing assessment age; it does not recover the original trading schedule. More windows and prospective observations are needed to assess persistence. A prospective comparison should fix the information and execution clocks before observing outcomes and record the analyst or fallback source for every decision. It should measure the outcomes of omitted calls and changed contracts as well as request cost and parse success. Appendix A distinguishes recorded implementation changes from offline tests, planned changes, and withheld sizing authority; post-change production outcomes remain untested.
